look_here_first: Start with the stout, often conspicuously LARGE upright perennial grass clump, then look for a terminal array of roughly two to five relatively long one-sided racemes. This species bears fairly LARGE, rounded to oval flattened spikelets (roughly 3.5–5 mm depending on treatment). A photograph of a green clump WITHOUT the inflorescence cannot settle a species call.

crew_field_steps: Recognize and photograph the sizeable erect broad-leaved bunch; current photo shows the leafy habit only.
Find a mature flowering head with multiple long one-sided racemes; count branches on a SINGLE culm and show complete axis.
Measure and photograph the relatively broad rounded oval spikelets with a mm ruler, and check leaf blade/sheath ligule before separating from dallisgrass and P. pubiflorum.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full flowering culm from base to complete mature seedhead.
Two mature racemes photographed from side and face with scale.
Broad oval mature spikelets plus glume/hair macro at mm scale.
Leaf sheath/collar membrane and vegetative habit paired with P. dilatatum.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Florida paspalum tends to have big coarse basal clumps with relatively few long racemes and large often rounded spikelets. Dallisgrass generally has conspicuous long silky hairs fringing its large spikelets; vaseygrass often has much more numerous finer racemes with smaller spikelets. P. pubiflorum commonly has smaller 2.7–3.2 mm spikelets, and pubescence needs careful comparison.
